kurals.tamil:
பகல்வெல்லும் கூகையைக் காக்கை இகல்வெல்லும்
வேந்தர்க்கு வேண்டும் பொழுது.
kurals.transliteration:
Pakalvellum Kookaiyaik Kaakkai Ikalvellum
Vendharkku Ventum Pozhudhu.
kurals.meaning: By day even a crow can beat the stronger owl. A king who means to beat his enemies must likewise wait for the time that favours him.
kurals.elementary: An owl is bigger and fiercer than a crow, but owls can hardly see in bright daylight. So in the daytime a crow can chase an owl away. If you pick the moment when you are at your best and the other side is at its weakest, even a small player can win.
kurals.university: The opening couplet grounds the chapter in natural observation. The kookai (owl) is stronger than the kaakkai (crow), but it is day-blind, so pakal (daytime) reverses their strength. Parimelazhagar draws the lesson for the vendhar (king): an ikal (hostile contest) is won not by strength alone but by the pozhudhu (hour) that suits one’s side. The image has a close Sanskrit parallel in the Panchatantra’s third book, the war of the crows and owls (Kākolūkīya), where the crows burn the owls’ cave by daylight. Both editions consulted (Thirukkural.net and Project Madurai) give the same text, apart from a sandhi spacing in ikalvellum.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Book III of the Panchatantra, the war of the crows and the owls, the owl-king’s army attacks the crows at night and slaughters them. The crow minister Sthirajivin later wins the owls’ trust and lives in their cave. Then, in daylight, when the owls are blind and helpless, he and the crows block the entrance and set it on fire, destroying the whole colony.
hinduism.explanation: The weaker crows cannot win by night, which is the owls’ hour. They win completely by choosing the day, when the owls cannot see.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s crow-and-owl image worked out as a full political fable.
hinduism.source: Panchatantra, Book III (Kākolūkīya, ‘Crows and Owls’), tr. Arthur W. Ryder
hinduism._accuracy_note: The same animals and the same daylight reversal. Paraphrased from the well-known frame story; Ryder’s wording was not rechecked this session.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then Jesus said unto them, My time is not yet come: but your time is alway ready.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus’ brothers urge him to show himself publicly in Judea at the feast. He refuses because the moment (kairos) is not yet right for him, though any time suits them.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s king, Jesus acts not when pressed to but when the hour favours his purpose.
christianity._accuracy_note: A real teaching on choosing the right time, but its setting is messianic mission rather than contest with an enemy.

islam.quote_or_event: At the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq, 627 CE), a much larger confederate army besieged Medina. The Muslims held their defensive line rather than meet it in open field. After weeks, a bitter cold wind at night wrecked the besiegers’ camp and they withdrew. The Qur’an recalls this in Sura 33:9, where God sent a wind and unseen forces against them.
islam.explanation: The weaker side avoided the stronger side’s favoured ground and waited until conditions turned against the besiegers.
islam.tie_back: As with the crow by day, victory came to the weaker side when circumstances were in its favour, not through raw strength.
islam.source: Qur’an 33:9–10 and the sira accounts of the Battle of the Trench
islam._accuracy_note: Islamic tradition credits the outcome to divine aid, not to human timing. The parallel is only in how conditions reversed relative strength.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And of the children of Issachar, which were men that had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do.”
judaism.explanation: When David was gathering support for his kingship, the Chronicler singles out the men of Issachar for one skill: they understood the times and so knew what Israel should do.
judaism.tie_back: The verse makes reading the moment a qualification of royal counsel, just as the Kural says kings need the right time.
judaism._accuracy_note: A direct statement that knowing the times guides political action. It has no crow-and-owl image.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Dhammaññu Sutta the Buddha lists seven qualities that make a monk worthy of gifts and respect. One of them is being kālaññū, ‘one who knows the right time’: the time for study, questioning, effort and seclusion.
buddhism.explanation: Knowing the proper time is counted as a distinct virtue, next to knowing the teaching, its meaning, oneself, moderation, assemblies and persons.
buddhism.tie_back: Kālaññutā is almost a Pali name for this chapter’s title, kaalam arithal (‘knowing the time’).
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.64 (Dhammaññu Sutta), tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: The concept matches closely, but the setting is monastic rather than royal. Sutta numbering differs between editions (7.64 or 7.68).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad Book 10, Odysseus and Diomedes scout the Trojan lines by night, when the Trojans and their new allies are asleep. They kill the Thracian king Rhesus and his men in their sleep and take his famous horses, which Achilles’ absence had left the Greeks unable to win in daylight battle.
greek_mythology.explanation: Having been beaten by day, the Greeks switch to the hour that favours stealth, and two men do what an army could not.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point in reverse lighting. Each side has its hour, and the wise fighter strikes in his own.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad, Book 10 (the Doloneia), tr. Samuel Butler
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear case of choosing the favourable hour. Unlike the Kural, the nocturnal predator here is the victor, not the day-creature.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “There is surely no greater wisdom, than well to time the beginnings, and onsets, of things.”
philosophy.explanation: In his essay on delays, Bacon calls the timing of beginnings the height of practical wisdom. He warns both against missing the moment and against acting before it is ripe.
philosophy.tie_back: Bacon states as a maxim what the Kural shows with the crow: the hour chosen decides the contest.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim from the Authorama public-domain text, and thematically almost identical.

kurals.tamil:
பருவத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல் திருவினைத்
தீராமை ஆர்க்குங் கயிறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Paruvaththotu Otta Ozhukal Thiruvinaith
Theeraamai Aarkkung Kayiru.
kurals.meaning: Acting in step with the season is the rope that ties Fortune down so she cannot slip away.
kurals.elementary: Farmers plant when the rains come, not whenever they like. If you do things at the right time, good luck stays with you as if tied by a rope. If you ignore the time, it wanders off.
kurals.university: Paruvam means season or ripe time, and otta ozhukal means conducting oneself so as to cling to it. The image in the second line is striking: thiru (Fortune, often personified as the goddess Lakshmi or Tirumakal) is fickle by nature, and timely action is the kayiru (rope) that aarkkum (binds) her so that she does not theeraamai, that is, depart. Parimelazhagar glosses paruvam as the time suited to the undertaking. He reads the couplet as a claim that wealth lasts only when action keeps pace with circumstance. Renaissance Europe has a close analogue in Machiavelli’s Fortuna, who favours the man whose conduct matches the times. The Tamil text is identical in both sources consulted.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let the king undertake his march in the fine month Margasirsha, or towards the months of Phalguna and Kaitra, according to the (condition of his) army.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu’s rules for kings give seasonal windows for campaigns, chosen to suit harvests and the readiness of the army.
hinduism.tie_back: This is paruvam in concrete form: royal success depends on moving with the season, not against it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified at sacred-texts.com. The context is military rather than general prosperity, but the principle of acting in season is exact.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.”
christianity.explanation: Paul uses the farmer’s image of harvest in its proper season to urge steady good work that will bear fruit at the right time.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul ties reward to season, although his focus is on endurance until the season comes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the seasonal-harvest logic. The Kural is about keeping worldly fortune, Paul about spiritual reward.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that there are two blessings in which many people are cheated: health and free time. People let both pass without using them, and later regret it.
islam.explanation: The hadith treats the right time to act as a gift that is easily wasted, not something always available.
islam.tie_back: The Kural adds that using the season well is exactly what keeps good fortune bound to you.
islam._accuracy_note: The Kural’s ‘season’ is paraphrased loosely as opportunity. The hadith’s emphasis is spiritual stewardship.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He [also] used to say: If I am not for myself, who is for me? But if I am for my own self [only], what am I? And if not now, when?”
judaism.explanation: Hillel’s three questions end by insisting that the present moment is the time to act, since postponement has no natural end.
judaism.tie_back: ‘If not now, when?’ is the moral core of keeping in step with the season.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim via Sefaria. Hillel stresses urgency, while the Kural stresses fit with the season; related but not identical.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The idler who does not exert himself when he should, who though young and strong is full of sloth, with a mind full of vain thoughts — such an indolent man does not find the path to wisdom.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada condemns the one who fails to make an effort at the time for effort (uṭṭhāna-kāla).
buddhism.tie_back: Missing the season for effort loses the prize, which is the Kural’s point about Fortune slipping loose.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified on Access to Insight. A good fit on timely effort, though the prize is wisdom rather than prosperity.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod’s farmer’s calendar tells Perses to start the harvest when the Pleiades rise and to plough when they set. It fixes each task to a sign in the sky and warns that the man who ploughs late will reap little.
greek_mythology.explanation: For Hesiod, prosperity comes to the one who keeps the gods’ seasons, and ruin to the one who acts out of time.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is paruvaththotu otta ozhukal, living in step with the season, as the path to lasting wealth.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days, lines 383–617 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel. Paraphrased; line references are approximate to the Loeb numbering.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In The Prince, chapter 25, Machiavelli argues that Fortune governs about half of human affairs. He says a prince prospers when his way of acting fits the times and falls when the times change and he does not.
philosophy.explanation: Machiavelli treats Fortune as a force that can be managed by matching one’s conduct to the quality of the times.
philosophy.tie_back: His Fortuna and Valluvar’s Thiru are the same fickle goddess, and both are held by timely conduct.
philosophy.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. XXV (tr. W. K. Marriott)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close conceptual match. Paraphrased; Marriott’s wording was not rechecked this session.

kurals.tamil:
அருவினை யென்ப உளவோ கருவியான்
காலம் அறிந்து செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aruvinai Yenpa Ulavo Karuviyaan
Kaalam Arindhu Seyin.
kurals.meaning: Is there any task that can really be called impossible, if one acts with the proper means and at the proper time?
kurals.elementary: Opening a tight jar is hard with bare hands. With the right tool and a little warm water it is easy. Most ‘impossible’ jobs become possible when you have the right tools and choose the right moment.
kurals.university: The couplet is a rhetorical question: aruvinai enpa ulavo, ‘are there things one could call hard deeds?’ The condition has two parts, karuviyaan (by means of instruments) and kaalam arindhu (knowing the time). Parimelazhagar takes karuvi to mean the resources of the state, such as army and treasury, together with the right methods. Neither timing without means nor means without timing is enough. The printed spelling ‘yenpa’ reflects sandhi with the preceding vowel; the word is enpa.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s Arthaśāstra, Book IX, opens with a chapter on knowing power, place and time before invading. It weighs the strength of counsel, treasury and army against the enemy’s, and also the seasons and terrain in which each force works best.
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya treats means (śakti) and time (kāla) as separate variables to be judged together before any undertaking.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s pairing of karuvi (means) and kaalam (time).
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book IX, Chapter 1 (tr. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Same doctrine of means plus time. Paraphrased from the chapter’s argument.

christianity.quote_or_event: “See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to be careful and to ‘buy up’ the opportune moment (exagorazomenoi ton kairon) rather than waste it.
christianity.tie_back: Wise, careful use of the moment is half of the Kural’s formula for making hard things achievable.
christianity._accuracy_note: Covers the timing half only. Nothing here corresponds to the Kural’s karuvi (means).

islam.quote_or_event: A man asked the Prophet whether he should leave his camel untied and trust in God, or tie it and trust. The Prophet told him to tie it and then trust.
islam.explanation: Reliance on God (tawakkul) is not a reason to neglect practical means. The two go together.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s success likewise needs the proper karuvi (means) as well as the favourable moment.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the means side well but has little to say about timing. The hadith is graded hasan by some scholars.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whoso keepeth the commandment shall feel no evil thing: and a wise man’s heart discerneth both time and judgment. Because to every purpose there is time and judgment…”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet says that every undertaking has its proper time and its proper manner (et u-mishpat), and that the wise person perceives both.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Time and judgment’ is a close Hebrew counterpart to the Kural’s ‘time and means’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in structure. Mishpat means method or procedure rather than material means.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Bhūmija Sutta the Buddha compares a person who seeks results by the wrong method to someone pressing sand for oil or milking a cow by its horn. With the right method, pressing sesame seeds or milking from the udder, the result comes whether one hopes for it or not.
buddhism.explanation: Results depend on using the right means. Wishing does not bring success and does not block it either.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s claim that nothing is hard for the one with proper karuvi rests on the same logic of fitting method to goal.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on means, silent on timing. The sutta’s real subject is the spiritual path.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Trapped in the Cyclops’ cave, Odysseus does not attack at once. He prepares an olive-wood stake, hardens it in the fire, gets Polyphemus drunk on strong wine, and blinds him only once the giant has fallen asleep.
greek_mythology.explanation: An impossible escape becomes possible through the right tools (stake, wine, a false name) used at the right moment (drunken sleep).
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s formula in story form: karuvi and kaalam together overcome a far stronger foe.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close illustration of means plus timing. Paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Further, there can be no doubt that a work is spoilt when not done at the right time? … the husbandman will not make his own plough or mattock, or other implements of agriculture, if they are to be good for anything.”
philosophy.explanation: Founding the first city in speech, Socrates argues that work is ruined if its moment is let slip, and that each worker needs good implements made by others, so smiths and carpenters must join the city.
philosophy.tie_back: The right time and the right implements, the Kural's kaalam and karuvi, appear together as the two conditions of successful work.
philosophy.source: Plato, Republic, Book II, 370b–c (tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett, Republic Book II); the ellipsis omits intervening dialogue. Plato pairs timing and tools in the context of the division of labour; he does not make the Kural's claim that with both nothing is impossible.

kurals.tamil:
ஞாலம் கருதினுங் கைகூடுங் காலம்
கருதி இடத்தாற் செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Gnaalam Karudhinung Kaikootung Kaalam
Karudhi Itaththaar Seyin.
kurals.meaning: Even if you aim at the whole world, it will come within your grasp, provided you choose the right time and act in the right place.
kurals.elementary: A surfer can ride a huge wave, but only by paddling out at the right moment and at the right spot. Pick the right time and place, and even very big goals become reachable.
kurals.university: Gnaalam karudhinum means ‘even if one sets one’s mind on the earth’, that is, universal dominion, and kaikoodum means ‘it will come into one’s hand’. The condition joins kaalam karudhi (considering the time) with idaththaal seyin (acting by means of the place). This anticipates the next chapter, Idanarithal (Knowing the Place, Kurals 491–500). Parimelazhagar explains that idam here means a place of action favourable to oneself and difficult for the enemy. Time and place are treated as the two coordinates of successful action, as in the kāla and deśa of Sanskrit statecraft. Both sources give identical text; ‘karudhinung’ carries the nasal sandhi of karudhinum before k-.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A widely quoted verse of Chāṇakya Nīti tells a person to think again and again about what the time is, who are friends, what the place is, what income and expenditure are, who one is, and what one’s strength is.
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya’s checklist puts time and place first among the questions to settle before acting.
hinduism.tie_back: The same two coordinates, kaalam and idam, are what the Kural says make even world-conquest possible.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased. Verse numbering varies across recensions of Chāṇakya Nīti.

christianity.quote_or_event: Speaking at the Areopagus in Athens, Paul says that God made all nations from one blood and fixed both their appointed times and the boundaries of where they live.
christianity.explanation: Paul presents history as ordered by the right times and the right places, under divine providence.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural gives the same two coordinates, time and place, as the conditions for great achievement.
christianity._accuracy_note: Only the pairing of time and place matches. Paul speaks of divine ordering, not human strategy.

islam.quote_or_event: After the Quraysh allies broke the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet marched on Mecca in 630 CE. He had gathered a large force secretly and approached from several directions at once. The city surrendered with almost no fighting.
islam.explanation: Years of patience were followed by a move at a well-chosen moment and by well-chosen routes, which won the Prophet’s central goal with little bloodshed.
islam.tie_back: Choosing the moment (the broken treaty) and the approach (several routes into Mecca) brought the greatest aim within reach, as the Kural promises.
islam.source: Qur’an 48 and 110; sira accounts of the Conquest of Mecca (Fath Makka)
islam._accuracy_note: Historical parallel, not a doctrinal teaching. Tradition credits the outcome to God’s help.

judaism.quote_or_event: “…and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?”
judaism.explanation: Mordecai urges Esther to act. She is now queen, in the one place (the Persian court) where she can save her people, at the one moment when it matters.
judaism.tie_back: Being in the right place at the right time turns an apparently impossible rescue into a real one.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified. Close on the time-and-place logic, although the book presents the timing as providential.

buddhism.quote_or_event: After his awakening, the Buddha at first hesitated to teach. When Brahmā Sahampati asked him, he surveyed the world and saw beings like lotuses at different stages of emergence from the water. Judging the time right, he went to the Deer Park at Isipatana to give his first sermon to the five ascetics, who were ready to understand.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha chose both the moment and the place and audience for the teaching that would spread across Asia.
buddhism.tie_back: A world-changing aim was achieved by judging kaalam and idam precisely.
buddhism.source: Saṃyutta Nikāya 6.1 (Āyācana Sutta) and the Vinaya Mahāvagga narrative
buddhism._accuracy_note: The aim here is spiritual, not political conquest. The parallel lies in the careful judgment of time and audience.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Zeus did not challenge Cronus while still a child hidden on Crete. He grew up in secret and freed his swallowed siblings. He then released the Cyclopes and Hundred-Handers from beneath the earth, gaining thunderbolts and allies, before fighting the Titans. He won rule of the cosmos.
greek_mythology.explanation: The eventual lord of the world waited for the time of his strength and chose his ground and allies before fighting.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Dominion over the world came through timing and position, as Valluvar says.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A cosmic myth, so the fit with the Kural’s political counsel is loose. Line ranges are approximate.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Without that opportunity their powers of mind would have been extinguished, and without those powers the opportunity would have come in vain.”
philosophy.explanation: Machiavelli says Moses, Cyrus, Romulus and Theseus owed nothing to fortune but opportunity: Cyrus, for example, had to find the Persians discontented with the Medes and the Medes softened by long peace before he could found his empire.
philosophy.tie_back: As in the Kural, the winning of great kingdoms depends on acting when time and circumstance are right.
philosophy.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. VI (tr. W. K. Marriott)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in Marriott's translation on Project Gutenberg (eBook #1232). Strong on time and opportunity as the condition of conquest; the Kural's 'place' is matched only loosely by Machiavelli's circumstances, not by terrain.

kurals.tamil:
காலம் கருதி இருப்பர் கலங்காது
ஞாலம் கருது பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaalam Karudhi Iruppar Kalangaadhu
Gnaalam Karudhu Pavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who aim at the world wait calmly, unshaken, watching for their time.
kurals.elementary: A cat watching a mouse-hole sits very still and doesn’t get upset or jump too early. People with big goals are like that. They stay calm and wait for their chance.
kurals.university: The couplet picks up gnaalam karudhu (‘aiming at the world’) from the previous kural and shows the inner attitude that goes with it. Such people iruppar, ‘stay’ or ‘sit still’, and do so kalangaadhu, ‘without being agitated’. Parimelazhagar explains that they are not disturbed by the enemy’s present prosperity or by their own present setbacks, because they know that the favourable time will come. The virtue described is patience that is also watchfulness, an active waiting rather than inertia. The printed division ‘karudhu pavar’ is a metrical split of karudhupavar, and the two sources agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When (the king) knows (that) at some future time his superiority (is) certain, and (that) at the time present (he will suffer) little injury, then let him have recourse to peaceful measures.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu advises a king who is sure to gain the upper hand later to stay at peace for now, since waiting costs him little.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s calm waiting for the right time, written as a rule of royal policy.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified at sacred-texts.com. Close doctrinal match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain.”
christianity.explanation: James uses the farmer who waits calmly for the rains as the model of patience before a great outcome.
christianity.tie_back: The waiting farmer matches the Kural’s unperturbed person who waits for the moment.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified. Same attitude, but the hope is eschatological rather than worldly.

islam.quote_or_event: At Hudaybiyyah (628 CE), the Prophet accepted a truce whose terms many companions found humiliating. They could not enter Mecca that year and had to return fugitives. The Qur’an nevertheless called it ‘a clear victory’ (48:1), and within two years Mecca opened to him.
islam.explanation: The Prophet held back from forcing the issue and waited calmly while circumstances turned in his favour.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s waiting ‘without agitation’ by one who aims at the greater goal.
islam.source: Qur’an 48:1; sira accounts of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
islam._accuracy_note: A strong historical parallel. The Islamic reading stresses trust in God as well as strategy.

judaism.quote_or_event: David was already anointed king by Samuel, yet he refused to seize the throne from Saul. For years he lived as a fugitive in the wilderness and twice spared Saul’s life when he had the chance to kill him, waiting for the kingship to come in its own time.
judaism.explanation: David’s restraint while marked for kingship is the Bible’s classic picture of patient waiting for one’s hour.
judaism.tie_back: He was one who ‘aimed at the realm’ and waited without panic for the right time.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close narrative fit. David’s motive is reverence for God’s anointed rather than tactics alone.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that as a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, the wise are not moved by praise or blame.
buddhism.explanation: The wise person keeps an inner steadiness whatever happens outside.
buddhism.tie_back: Kalangaadhu, ‘unshaken’, names the same calm that the Kural requires while waiting.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the calm but not the strategic waiting for a moment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: For years Penelope held off the suitors. She promised to choose one of them after finishing a shroud for Laertes, and each night she secretly unwove what she had woven by day. She kept the household intact until Odysseus returned.
greek_mythology.explanation: She could not overpower the suitors, so she bought time with calm cunning, waiting for the moment when things would change.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope shows the Kural’s patient waiting, steady amid pressure and alert to the coming time.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good fit for patient waiting, but her aim is to protect the household, not to win dominion.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Sun Tzu said: The good fighters of old first put themselves beyond the possibility of defeat, and then waited for an opportunity of defeating the enemy.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu teaches that security lies in your own hands, while the chance of victory must be waited for, since the enemy provides it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s picture: secure and unshaken, the aspirant waits for the time.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War IV.1 (tr. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim from suntzusaid.com (Giles). A near-identical strategic doctrine.

kurals.tamil:
ஊக்க முடையான் ஒடுக்கம் பொருதகர்
தாக்கற்குப் பேருந் தகைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Ookka Mutaiyaan Otukkam Porudhakar
Thaakkarkup Perun Thakaiththu.
kurals.meaning: When an energetic man holds back, it is like a fighting ram stepping back so that it can charge harder.
kurals.elementary: When a ram wants to butt, it first walks backward a few steps, then rushes forward with great force. A strong person who waits quietly for a while is not giving up. They are getting ready to charge.
kurals.university: Ookkam means energy or zeal, and otukkam means drawing in, withdrawal or restraint. Porudhakar is a fighting ram (poru, ‘fight’, + thakar, ‘ram’), and thaakkal means butting or striking. Perum thakaiththu means ‘is of the nature of drawing back’, which Parimelazhagar reads as backing up to strike harder. The image reassures anyone who might misread the patient man’s restraint as weakness: his pause is how he gathers force. The same logic appears in the feigned retreats of military history and in Sun Tzu’s ‘coyness of a maiden’ followed by the rush of a hare. The printed ‘perun thakaiththu’ shows the nasal sandhi of perum before th-.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Jarasandha besieged Mathura again and again, Krishna and Balarama finally withdrew. They moved the Yadavas to the island fortress of Dwaraka, so that Krishna came to be called Ranchhod, ‘the one who left the battlefield’. From that secure base Krishna later arranged Jarasandha’s death through Bhima.
hinduism.explanation: The withdrawal looked like flight but was a strategic step back that made a decisive later blow possible.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the ram stepping back before the charge: an energetic hero’s retreat that sets up the strike.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close in spirit. The epithet Ranchhod comes from later devotional tradition, not the Purāṇa text itself.

christianity.quote_or_event: When the Pharisees plotted to destroy Jesus, Matthew says he knew of it and withdrew from there. Great crowds followed him and he healed them, and he told them not to make him known, since his hour had not yet come.
christianity.explanation: Jesus repeatedly avoided confrontation that would have come too early, and kept his mission going until the appointed time.
christianity.tie_back: His withdrawal is restraint in the service of a later and greater purpose, like the ram’s step back.
christianity._accuracy_note: The withdrawal-before-the-hour pattern fits. There is no ‘charge’ in the military sense.

islam.quote_or_event: Facing persecution in Mecca, the Prophet and his followers emigrated to Medina in 622 CE (the Hijra). There they built a community and strength. Eight years later they returned to Mecca in triumph.
islam.explanation: The Hijra was a withdrawal that became the base for later success. Islam dates its calendar from it.
islam.tie_back: Like the ram’s backward step, the retreat to Medina gathered the force for the return.
islam.source: Qur’an 9:40; sira accounts of the Hijra
islam._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel. Muslims see the Hijra primarily as obedience to God, not as tactics.

judaism.quote_or_event: At Ai, Joshua set an ambush behind the city and led the main army in a feigned flight. When the men of Ai left their walls to pursue, the ambush took the city, and Israel turned back and struck.
judaism.explanation: The pretended retreat drew the enemy out of his strong position so that Israel’s counter-attack would be decisive.
judaism.tie_back: This is the fighting ram’s step back turned into a battle plan.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: withdrawal followed by a stronger blow.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kumma Sutta, a tortoise draws its limbs and head into its shell when a jackal comes near. The jackal waits for it to put something out, but the tortoise keeps still until the jackal gives up and leaves. The Buddha tells monks to guard their senses in the same way.
buddhism.explanation: Drawing in at the dangerous moment protects one from a waiting predator.
buddhism.tie_back: Otukkam, drawing in, is shown as strength rather than weakness, though here it protects and does not strike.
buddhism.source: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.199 (Kumma Sutta), tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of restraint as wise self-withdrawal. It lacks the Kural’s following charge.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After ten years of fighting, the Greeks burned their camp and sailed away to hide behind the island of Tenedos, leaving the wooden horse on the shore. When the Trojans had brought it inside, the fleet came back by night and the men in the horse opened the gates.
greek_mythology.explanation: The apparent withdrawal was the preparation for the blow that ended the war.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The ram steps back and then charges. The Greeks retreat and then take Troy.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 8.492–520 (Demodocus’ song); fuller in Virgil, Aeneid II
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close fit. The retreat to Tenedos is detailed in Virgil rather than Homer.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “At first, then, exhibit the coyness of a maiden, until the enemy gives you an opening; afterwards emulate the rapidity of a running hare, and it will be too late for the enemy to oppose you.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu advises apparent passivity until the enemy exposes himself, then sudden, overwhelming speed.
philosophy.tie_back: Restraint first and then a rush is the ram’s backward step and forward charge.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War XI.68 (tr. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim from suntzusaid.com (Giles). Nearly identical logic.

kurals.tamil:
பொள்ளென ஆங்கே புறம்வேரார் காலம்பார்த்து
உள்வேர்ப்பர் ஒள்ளி யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pollena Aange Puramveraar Kaalampaarththu
Ulverppar Olli Yavar.
kurals.meaning: The wise do not blaze up in anger on the spot. They keep it inside and wait for the right time.
kurals.elementary: If someone is rude to you and you shout back at once, you may make things worse. A wise person stays calm on the outside, remembers what happened, and deals with it later at a better moment.
kurals.university: Pollena means suddenly or at once, and aange means right there. Puram veraar means ‘they do not sweat or seethe outwardly’, and ul verppar means ‘they seethe within’. Olliyavar are the bright or clear-minded. Parimelazhagar explains that when the wise are provoked by enemies, they do not show anger immediately, because doing so would warn the enemy. They hold it until kaalam paarththu, ‘watching for the time’. The couplet is about strategy, not ethical renunciation of anger: the feeling is kept and redirected, not dissolved. Commentators contrast it with Chapter 31 (Vekulaamai, ‘Not Being Angry’), where anger is to be given up entirely. The two sources agree; ‘olli yavar’ is a metrical split of olliyavar.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the dice hall, as Draupadi was humiliated, Bhima raged. Yudhishthira’s word, and the Pandavas’ bond to the wager, held him back from attacking the Kauravas then and there. Instead Bhima swore vows he fulfilled thirteen years later at Kurukshetra, breaking Duryodhana’s thigh and drinking Duhshasana’s blood.
hinduism.explanation: Bhima’s anger was not given up but held in until the war, the right time.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘seething within, not without’, kept until the moment for revenge came.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Sabhā Parva (Dyūta sub-parva) and Śalya/Karṇa Parvas (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close fit to anger held for the right time. The epic’s moral view of Bhima’s violence is ambivalent.

christianity.quote_or_event: James tells believers to be swift to hear, slow to speak and slow to wrath, because human anger does not produce the righteousness of God.
christianity.explanation: Early Christian ethics warns against quick, uncontrolled outbursts of anger.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Slow to wrath’ matches the Kural’s refusal to blaze up on the spot, though James does not advise saving it for later.
christianity._accuracy_note: Only the restraint matches. The Kural’s strategic holding of anger for later has no parallel in James.

islam.quote_or_event: “˹They are˺ those who donate in prosperity and adversity, control their anger, and pardon others. And Allah loves the good-doers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises al-kāẓimīn al-ghayẓ, literally ‘those who hold in their rage’, as a camel swallows back its cud.
islam.tie_back: Kaẓm al-ghayẓ, holding in rage, is almost a literal counterpart of ul verppar, ‘seething within’.
islam.source: Qur’an 3:134 (tr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on quran.com. The same inner holding-in, but the Qur’an moves toward forgiveness, not a later strike.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Joseph made haste; for his bowels did yearn upon his brother: and he sought where to weep; and he entered into his chamber, and wept there. And he washed his face, and went out, and refrained himself, and said, Set on bread.”
judaism.explanation: Overcome by feeling at seeing Benjamin, Joseph hides it, weeps in private, then returns composed. He does not yet reveal himself to the brothers who sold him, and waits until the test is complete.
judaism.tie_back: This is powerful feeling hidden within and held back until the right moment, as the Kural describes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified. The emotion is love and grief rather than anger, but the timing discipline is the same.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada calls the one who checks rising anger, as a charioteer checks a rolling chariot, a true charioteer. Others merely hold the reins.
buddhism.explanation: Mastery means stopping anger at the very moment it starts to roll.
buddhism.tie_back: The check on the sudden outburst (pollena) is shared, though Buddhism aims to extinguish anger, not store it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the restraint only. The Buddhist goal of letting go of anger diverges from the Kural’s strategic intent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Agamemnon takes Briseis, Achilles half-draws his sword to kill him. Athena, visible to him alone, grips his hair and tells him to hold his hand, to use words only, and promises that he will one day receive gifts three times as great for this insult. Achilles pushes the sword back into its sheath.
greek_mythology.explanation: The goddess of wisdom stops the instant outburst and points Achilles toward a later redress.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural exactly: the wise do not strike on the spot but hold their wrath for the right time.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle praises the man who is angry at the right things and with the right people, and also as he ought, when he ought and for as long as he ought. He blames both irascibility and a slavish lack of spirit.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, anger is not bad in itself. Its virtue is a matter of right measure and right timing.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wise man also keeps his anger but lets it out only ‘when he ought’.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.5, 1125b31–1126a3 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual match on the timing of anger. Paraphrased from Ross.

kurals.tamil:
செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க இறுவரை
காணின் கிழக்காம் தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Serunaraik Kaanin Sumakka Iruvarai
Kaanin Kizhakkaam Thalai.
kurals.meaning: When you meet your foes, bear with them, even show them deference. When their time of downfall comes, their heads will roll.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes you have to put up with someone difficult who is stronger than you right now. If you stay patient, a time will come when they lose their power. Wait for that time instead of starting a fight you can’t win.
kurals.university: Serunar are enemies, and sumakka means ‘carry’ or ‘bear’. Parimelazhagar understands this as even showing them deference, carrying them ‘on one’s head’ as it were. Iruvarai is the limit or end-time, the point at which the enemy’s fortune has run out. Kizhakkaam thalai, ‘the head will turn downward’, comes from kizh (below). Parimelazhagar reads kizhakku here as keezh, ‘downward’, not the homonym meaning ‘east’. The advice is openly realpolitik: submit outwardly while weak and strike when the enemy’s time has come. It closely echoes Kanika’s counsel to Dhritarashtra in the Mahābhārata to carry the enemy on one’s shoulder and then smash him like a pot on a stone. Both sources give identical text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The minister Kanika advises Dhritarashtra that as long as time is unfavourable, a king should carry his foe on his shoulder. When the right time comes, he should dash the foe to pieces like an earthen pot thrown on a stone.
hinduism.explanation: Kanika’s Machiavellian counsel, given as the Kauravas turn against the Pandavas, recommends outward submission until the moment to destroy.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘Carry him on your shoulder’ is sumakka, ‘bear him’. The pot smashed on the stone is the head that falls at iruvarai.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Ādi Parva, Section 142 (Kanika’s counsel; tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Nearly identical image and doctrine. Paraphrased; section numbering follows Ganguli and differs in the Critical Edition.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the wheat and the tares, the householder refuses to pull up the weeds too early and waits for harvest, when they can be removed safely.
christianity.tie_back: Enduring what is hostile until its appointed end is the Kural’s sumakka … iruvarai.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified. The patience-until-the-end structure matches, but the judgment is divine and eschatological, not a king’s plan.

islam.quote_or_event: In an early Meccan sura, the Prophet is told to bear patiently what his opponents say and to part from them gracefully. God says to leave the wealthy deniers to Him and to give them a little respite.
islam.explanation: The weak early community is told to endure hostility and not to retaliate, because the opponents’ end is fixed.
islam.tie_back: Bearing the enemy now and trusting that his downfall will come in its time is the Kural’s counsel.
islam._accuracy_note: Close in structure. In the Qur’an the retribution belongs to God, not to the one who waits.

judaism.quote_or_event: “David said furthermore, As the LORD liveth, the LORD shall smite him; or his day shall come to die; or he shall descend into battle, and perish.”
judaism.explanation: David, standing over the sleeping Saul, refuses to kill him. He is sure that Saul’s appointed end will come by itself.
judaism.tie_back: ‘His day shall come’ is very nearly the Kural’s iruvarai, the boundary-time of the enemy’s fall.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified. An excellent match on bearing the foe until his fixed end, though David will not strike himself.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta repeatedly plotted against the Buddha. He tried to have him killed by assassins, a boulder and a maddened elephant. The Buddha never retaliated. Tradition says Devadatta was finally swallowed by the earth as the result of his own deeds.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha bore his enemy’s hostility, and the enemy fell by the working of his own karma.
buddhism.tie_back: This shares the Kural’s pattern of enduring now until the enemy’s end, without the Kural’s idea of striking back.
buddhism.source: Vinaya, Cullavagga VII; Dhammapada Commentary on verse 17
buddhism._accuracy_note: Only the structure matches. The Buddhist ethic rejects the Kural’s strategic hostility.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Returning to Ithaca disguised as a beggar, Odysseus endures the suitors’ insults, a stool thrown at him, and the taunts of his own disloyal servants. He waits until the contest of the bow puts a weapon in his hands. Then he throws off his rags and kills them all.
greek_mythology.explanation: The king bears humiliation from his enemies in his own hall until the moment of their ruin comes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is sumakka followed by the falling heads, in the most famous revenge story of Greek epic.

philosophy.quote_or_event: After Rome’s disasters against Hannibal, Quintus Fabius Maximus refused pitched battle and shadowed the invader from the hills. He endured public mockery as ‘Hannibal’s pedagogue’ and ‘the Delayer’ (Cunctator) while Hannibal’s strength wore down. Plutarch praises his judgment, which Rome’s later victory vindicated.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch holds up Fabius as the model of the statesman who bears an enemy’s presence and his own disgrace until time turns the balance.
philosophy.tie_back: Fabius ‘carried’ Hannibal in Italy for years until the invader’s power ran out, as the Kural advises.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Historical-moral parallel from Plutarch. Paraphrased and chapter references approximate.

kurals.tamil:
எய்தற் கரியது இயைந்தக்கால் அந்நிலையே
செய்தற் கரிய செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Eydhar Kariyadhu Iyaindhakkaal Annilaiye
Seydhar Kariya Seyal.
kurals.meaning: When a rare opportunity arrives, seize it at once and do the deed that would otherwise be too hard to do.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a gate that opens only for a moment. If you run through right away, you get in. If you wait to think it over, it shuts. When a rare chance comes, use it straight away.
kurals.university: The couplet uses a chiasmus of ‘rare’ things: eydhar kariyadhu (what is hard to obtain, the rare opportunity) and seydhar kariya seyal (deeds hard to do). The link is annilaiye, ‘in that very state, at that very moment’. Iyaindhakkaal means ‘when it has come together’ or ‘when it has fallen into place’. Parimelazhagar stresses immediacy: the opportunity will not return, so the difficult act must be done while it lasts. The previous couplets counselled patience, and this one completes them by insisting that patience ends in decisive action. The Greek figure of Kairos, bald behind so that he cannot be grabbed once he has passed, is the classic Western emblem of the same idea. Text identical in both sources; ‘eydhar kariyadhu’ and ‘seydhar kariya’ are metrical splits of eydharkariyadhu and seydharkariya.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna tells Arjuna that fortunate are the warriors who meet, unsought, a righteous war like this one, which comes as an open door to heaven. To turn away from it would be to lose both duty and honour.
hinduism.explanation: The battle has arrived by itself (yadṛcchayā) as a rare chance for the kshatriya, and to hesitate is to fail.
hinduism.tie_back: A rare, unsought opportunity that must be taken at once matches the Kural’s eydharkariyadhu iyaindhakkaal.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good fit on seizing a rare chance. The Gītā frames it as dharma rather than advantage.

christianity.quote_or_event: “…behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.”
christianity.explanation: Paul quotes Isaiah to insist that the moment of grace is now and should not be put off.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Now is the accepted time’ carries the urgency of the Kural’s annilaiye, ‘at that very moment’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified. Same urgency about a rare moment, but the opportunity is spiritual.

islam.quote_or_event: Ibn ‘Umar, recalling the Prophet’s counsel to live in the world like a stranger, advised: if you reach the evening, do not wait for the morning, and if you reach the morning, do not wait for the evening. Take from your health for your sickness, and from your life for your death.
islam.explanation: Present opportunities are fleeting and should be used now, before they are gone.
islam.tie_back: Using the chance while it lasts is the Kural’s annilaiye, ‘then and there’.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the urgency. The focus is otherworldly preparation rather than worldly feats.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Say not: ‘when I shall have leisure I shall study;’ perhaps you will not have leisure.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel warns against putting off what matters until a better time that may never arrive.
judaism.tie_back: The chance you have is the one to use, as the Kural says of the rare opportunity.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified via Sefaria. Same warning against delay, applied to Torah study.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a border city is closely guarded both within and without, even so, guard yourself. Do not let slip this opportunity (for spiritual growth). For those who let slip this opportunity grieve indeed when consigned to hell.”
buddhism.explanation: The Pali khaṇo vo mā upaccagā, ‘let not the moment pass you by’, treats human birth as a rare opportunity that must not be wasted.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s rare moment, eydharkariyadhu, that must be seized annilaiye, then and there.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified on Access to Insight. Very close on the rare, fleeting opportunity.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Kairos, the god of the opportune moment, was portrayed in Lysippus’ famous bronze. A dialogue epigram attributed to Posidippus describes it. The god stands on tiptoe on a razor’s edge with wings on his feet and a lock of hair over his forehead, while the back of his head is bald. Whoever meets him must grab him from the front, because once he has passed no one can catch him from behind.
greek_mythology.explanation: Kairos personifies the fleeting right moment that must be seized at once or lost forever.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘when the rare thing comes, act then’ is the exact moral of the Kairos statue.
greek_mythology.source: Posidippus, epigram on Lysippus’ Kairos (Greek Anthology 16.275)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near-perfect conceptual match. The statue is described from the epigram and later ekphrases.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar, Brutus argues for marching at once to Philippi. He says there is a tide in human affairs which, if taken at its flood, leads to fortune, and if missed leaves life stranded in shallows and misery.
philosophy.explanation: Brutus insists that a favourable moment, once missed, does not come back.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s rare opportunity is Shakespeare’s flood tide, and both must be taken the moment it comes.
philosophy.source: William Shakespeare, Julius Caesar, Act 4, Scene 3
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close thematic match. Ironically, Brutus’ own timing proves fatal at Philippi. Paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
கொக்கொக்க கூம்பும் பருவத்து மற்றதன்
குத்தொக்க சீர்த்த இடத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Kokkokka Koompum Paruvaththu Matradhan
Kuththokka Seerththa Itaththu.
kurals.meaning: While the time is not right, stay still like a heron. When the moment is ripe, strike as fast and as surely as its beak.
kurals.elementary: Have you seen a heron fishing? It stands very still in the water for a long time. When a fish swims close, it stabs down in a flash. Be patient like the heron while you wait, and quick like the heron when your chance comes.
kurals.university: The chapter ends with a double simile built on the kokku (heron or crane). In the season of koompum, ‘folding in’ or ‘drawing oneself together’, one should kokku okka, ‘be like the heron’, standing motionless and seemingly asleep. When the time is seerththa, ‘excellent’ or ‘fitting’, one should be like its kuththu (stab). Parimelazhagar notes the pairing of stillness and sudden strike as the model of a king’s conduct toward enemies. The heron also appears in Manusmṛti 7.106 and in the Chāṇakya Nīti as a model of patient concentration, which suggests a shared South Asian stock image. Some texts, including the musical setting on Thirukkural.net, read ‘seerththa vidaththu’ with a glide consonant. The two editions consulted print ‘seerththa idaththu’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him plan his undertakings (patiently meditating) like a heron; like a lion, let him put forth his strength; like a wolf, let him snatch (his prey); like a hare, let him double in retreat.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu’s rules for kings use animal models, and the heron stands for patient, concentrated planning before the strike.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s heron-king, still in planning and swift in the snatch.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified at sacred-texts.com. The same bird and the same royal context.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take ye heed, watch and pray: for ye know not when the time is.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples to stay alert and ready, because the decisive moment will come without warning.
christianity.tie_back: The heron’s watchful stillness before an unpredictable moment is the attitude described here.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified. It shares watchful readiness but has no idea of a strike.

islam.quote_or_event: At Uhud (625 CE) the Prophet posted archers on a hill with orders not to leave it. When they abandoned their post to collect spoils, Khalid ibn al-Walid, then fighting for Mecca, who had been watching for exactly that gap, struck the Muslims from the rear. The Qur’an (3:152) reflects on the lapse.
islam.explanation: The episode shows both sides of the heron’s lesson: the cost of leaving watchful stillness too early, and the power of a strike timed to the enemy’s opening.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an’s reproach for abandoning the post and Khalid’s timed charge together illustrate the Kural’s wait-then-strike.
islam.source: Qur’an 3:152; sira accounts of the Battle of Uhud
islam._accuracy_note: Indirect. The lesson is drawn from a Muslim setback, not from a teaching about herons or timing as such.

judaism.quote_or_event: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven… a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet’s poem of times pairs opposite actions, each right in its own season.
judaism.tie_back: The heron’s time of stillness and time of striking are one of Kohelet’s pairs in bird form.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified. The classic statement of timing in the Hebrew Bible, a strong thematic summary for the whole chapter.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Abhaya Sutta, the Buddha says that the Tathāgata knows the proper time to say even unwelcome things that are true and beneficial. He compares himself to a person who quickly removes a stick or stone from an infant’s mouth, even if it draws blood, when the moment requires it.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha waits for the right time (kālaññū) and then acts decisively, even painfully, for the good of the other.
buddhism.tie_back: Holding back until the right moment and then acting sharply is the heron’s pattern, applied to speech.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikāya 58 (Abhaya Sutta), tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: Timing-then-decisive-action matches. The context is compassionate speech, not dealing with enemies.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Gaia hid her son Cronus in ambush with a jagged sickle. When Ouranos came at night and lay over the earth, Cronus struck in a single blow and overthrew his father.
greek_mythology.explanation: Cronus waited hidden and motionless for the one moment when his far stronger father was exposed, then struck decisively.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Still in ambush and swift in the strike, Cronus follows the heron’s method.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear wait-then-strike structure. The myth is violent and not offered as a model of virtue.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “…it is good, to commit the beginnings of all great actions to Argus, with his hundred eyes, and the ends to Briareus, with his hundred hands; first to watch, and then to speed.”
philosophy.explanation: Bacon divides action into a phase of watchful vigilance and a phase of swift execution. He adds that ‘secrecy in the counsel, and celerity in the execution’ make the statesman effective.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘First to watch, and then to speed’ is the heron’s stillness followed by its stab.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim from the Authorama public-domain text. An almost exact conceptual twin of the Kural.
